turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Thursday, the twelfth of November. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Nayib Bukele says his soldiers destroyed a gang headquarters outside Port-au-Prince. [pause] Most of them are not under anybody's mandate.
[curious] Not under— we'll come back to that. The biggest share offering ever attempted was registered on Tuesday, and the companies buying it are the ones selling the buyer its chips.
And American inflation came in hot, so the Federal Reserve is now priced to raise rates next month. Not cut. Raise.
[thoughtful] That's a different world from the one we were in a fortnight ago.
It is. Haiti first.
Right. What actually happened?

Bukele posted video on Tuesday the tenth showing helicopters over Croix-des-Bouquets, outside Port-au-Prince. He said Salvadoran forces had destroyed the house and the headquarters of a gang leader called Wilson Joseph. About two thousand Salvadoran troops have been there since mid-October. The United Nations authorised a gang-suppression force. The U.N. spokesman said on the third of November that about two hundred of the Salvadorans operate under it.
[pause] Two hundred of two thousand.
The other eighteen hundred answer to San Salvador. Under a bilateral agreement neither government will publish.
So if you're a Haitian and a soldier does something to you —
There's no public text saying when they may shoot, or who you complain to. That's Amnesty International's point, and they've asked for the agreement to be made public.
[sighs] Okay. What does Bukele say it is?

He was explicit in October. Quote — this is not an operation against the Haitian people, nor an invasion of the country of Haiti. And: we do not come to Haiti to make money, because nobody is paying us for this. He says El Salvador covers ninety per cent of the cost.
Which is a strange thing to volunteer for.
The analysts think that's the story. A Salvadoran strategist, Roberto Dubon, calls it — quote — an election campaign to promote Nayib Bukele and present him as if he were a superhero.
[wry] Subtle.
He also says Bukele is using Haiti as a testing ground. Diego Da Rin at the International Crisis Group warns the troops' eagerness for quick symbolic victories carries enormous risks for civilians.
And El Salvador votes when? [deadpan] No connection, I'm sure.

Now. There's a number everybody is printing and we are not. Twenty dead in that operation. Al Jazeera put it in the headline. But France Twenty-Four says plainly it comes from the Miami Herald citing unnamed sources — and U.P.I. read Bukele's own post and reports it gave no casualty figure at all.
So one newspaper's anonymous sources.
We're not printing it as a fact.
[warmly] Good.

There's also a Dominican analyst, Humberto Salazar, who says the reported timing doesn't match the video — the strike was put at half past two in the morning, and the explosions are in daylight. Unverified. And no Salvadoran response has been published. We printed that he said it, and that it's unverified.
What would settle any of it?
A body count from Haiti's own police, and publication of that agreement.
One more from the desk — the strange one.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it destroyed navigation equipment on Didamar, an uninhabited Omani island in the Strait of Hormuz. A senior Omani official says the lights were never touched.
[gasps] The country that owns the rock says nothing happened?
Satellite imagery that morning shows no obvious damage. Reuters verified smoke and a heat signature and could confirm nothing else.
So Tehran is claiming an attack that the victim denies.
On the territory of the one Gulf state trying very hard not to take a side.
Right — money. And you said raise.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics published October's inflation on Tuesday morning. Prices up four tenths of a per cent on the month. Core — strip out food and energy — up three tenths. It's the third month running at three tenths. No improvement. Two hours before the print, in London, the governor Christopher Waller said he was — quote — leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of twenty-five basis points in December.
[gasps] An increase.
And he added that a reading around three tenths or higher would mean a half-point rise should be considered.
And it printed at exactly three tenths.
Exactly. The market now puts a quarter-point rise at eighty-eight point eight per cent, and a half-point at eleven point two.
[exhales] From nothing.

Here's the part I keep turning over. Nobody can say what inflation has done over the past year. The statistics agency didn't collect October of last year. Funding lapse. So twelve-month changes can't be computed for most series.
[drawn out] They're about to make the biggest monetary decision in two years without a year-ago comparison.
Three surviving lines. Petrol, new cars, used cars. That's it.
All right, explain the mechanism, because four things are doing four different things.
One force. Over six sessions the ten-year real yield — the return after expected inflation — rose eighteen basis points. And expected inflation fell fourteen.
So the whole move is real.
More than all of it. That's a market that believes the tightening will work, not one frightened of inflation.
And a real risk-free rate is a charge on anything that pays you nothing.

Gold closed Wednesday below four thousand dollars. Down about six per cent this year, about twenty-six below its January peak. Bitcoin's down about fourteen. Both of them. Gold and bitcoin are among this year's worst major assets — which hasn't happened before.
[thoughtful] So much for store of value.

When the risk-free real rate is two point seven eight, store of value isn't a category that protects you. It's a category that pays you nothing. Went up. Global equities rose one and a half per cent on Wednesday, on news that made the artificial-intelligence build-out look like it can fund itself.
So bonds are pricing the cost of money and shares are pricing something else entirely.

And the two never met. That's the fragility. Not advice, by the way — explanation. The police have confirmed an investigation into a company called Megaspeed, registered at Ocean Financial Centre on Collyer Quay. It's an Nvidia customer. Nvidia's board has opened its own inquiry into whether its chief executive was targeted by a foreign intelligence service, and the alleged conduit is Megaspeed's former managing director.
[gasps] And the numbers?
Assets went from thirty-three million U.S. dollars in twenty twenty-three to three billion in twenty twenty-four. On paid-up capital of ten million.
Is Singapore the chip-smuggling hub, then?
Here's the sceptic, and it's strong. Over ninety-nine per cent of the revenue billed to Singapore from controlled data-centre products in one quarter was for customers based in the United States.
So the invoices are here —
And the machines are somewhere else. A country that looks like it's buying an enormous quantity of chips is mostly a country issuing an enormous quantity of invoices.
Has anyone been charged?
Not Megaspeed. And the Home Affairs Ministry flatly denies the central claim — it says there were no investigations in respect of the person named.
That's not a no comment. Technology. The offering.

Anthropic filed an amendment on Tuesday registering up to seventy-four billion dollars of stock at a maximum of seventy-eight dollars a share. If it prices in that range it's the largest stock-market debut ever attempted. Exhibit ten point one five is a share purchase agreement with Google. Ten billion dollars.
Google, which also sells it computing capacity.
Reports put the total private placement at twenty-six billion with Nvidia matching, and others alongside. Only the Google leg is confirmed in the filings.
[thoughtful] So the people selling the shovels have bought into the mine.
And on the other side of the ledger sit about nine hundred billion dollars of committed payments — substantially all of it for computing.
Is anybody defending the valuation?
Not loudly. One commenter — handle cmiles eight — notes the figure has walked down from two trillion to one and a half to possibly one, and says Anthropic doesn't own compute, it rents it.
And the honest caveat?

Every number in that thread is an unverified commenter's claim. We printed none of them as fact. And we printed a disclosure, because the company in question makes the model this edition was assembled with.
[warmly] Say that out loud, always. Home lab. You had something that made me laugh.
Sixty-four gigabytes of ordinary desktop memory, at a British retailer on Wednesday, cost one thousand one hundred and thirty-nine pounds.
That's… more than a graphics card.
More than their cheapest current top-tier card, yes.
[scoffs] What happened?

The data centres are bidding first. And the older, slower memory standard is now trading about a third above the newer one, per bit. For anyone running large models at home it inverts the usual advice. The cheap part of the machine has become the expensive part.
Anything to cheer us up?

An American outfit published a sixty-five-billion-parameter model under a genuinely open licence, small enough for one machine. The community conversion has been downloaded about twelve times more than the official weights.
[amused] Which tells you how people actually run these things. The Kit, quickly.

Sigma's new camera shipped Wednesday. Two thousand eight hundred and eighty-eight Singapore dollars. Full frame, three hundred and seventy-six grams, no grip, no viewfinder in the box, and no mechanical shutter at all. Eighty-nine per cent and a Silver award from the reviewer who actually measured it. But he also found the high-dynamic-range processing cannot be switched off, and says it can be deeply unflattering on light-skinned portraits.
[wry] A camera with opinions.

And the Atelier. The maker of the day is a Japanese pottery called Motoshige, in Shimane, founded nineteen twenty-five. The suribachi — the Japanese mortar. Its interior is combed with fine radiating grooves, cut by hand into the clay before firing. The forming and glazing are mechanised. The grooves are not. Their distributors say so plainly.
What does it cost?
Four hundred and sixty-two yen. About four Singapore dollars.
[gasps] Four?
An American boutique sells the same workshop's bowl for forty-three dollars fifty, with the maker's name stripped off the page.
[laughs] That's the whole desk in one sentence.

And the sceptic's just as good. America's Test Kitchen timed it and found no fragrance difference at all between mortar-ground and machine-ground pepper. Not entirely. The mortar genuinely wins on wet pastes — pesto, rempah, curry paste. It ties on dry spices. If you only grind spices, buy a blade grinder.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning.
[laughs] What have we got?
Change ringing. English church bells.
[curious] The permutation thing.
The permutation thing. And the peg is that on Monday, British ringers begin counting themselves for the first time since nineteen eighty-eight.
Start with the mechanics, because I've never understood it.

An English tower bell is bolted to a wheel about the width of a small table, and it swings all the way over — mouth up to mouth up — and back. And the person pulling the rope is standing on a floor below. They cannot see the bell at all.
[whispers] Half a tonne of bronze, by feel.
Median tenor bell, across all the ringable rings in the world, is about five hundred and forty-six kilograms.
So why permutations and not tunes?
Inertia. Each bell can only move one place at a time in the order. You physically cannot play a melody.
So they did maths instead.
Every bell sounds once per row. Each row differs from the last by swapping neighbours. The patterns are called methods, and there are more than twenty-three thousand of them in the official library.
And a peal is?
Five thousand and forty changes. Which is seven factorial — every possible order of seven bells, exactly once. About three hours. No break, no written aids, nobody substituted.
[exhales] Three hours.
Two from this month. Harlow, the seventh of November — three hours and three minutes. Brailsford, the sixth — two hours fifty.
What does the gear cost? Because this is usually where you tell me somebody's spent a fortune.
Here's what's strange. You can't buy the instrument. A ring of bells belongs to a church.
So there's nothing to buy.

Handbells. A new twelve from the successor to the Whitechapel foundry is five thousand eight hundred and ninety-eight pounds plus tax. A good used set is three thousand two hundred and fifty. A beautiful set can be the wrong set. Bells voiced for tunes hum too long — change ringers want a drier strike so you can hear the rhythm. The clappers are even set differently.
[thoughtful] So you can't hear the fault in the shop.
Beyond that it's twenty pounds of software and nothing else. Total honest spend to become competent: about a hundred and ten pounds.
Then what's the actual cost?
Tuesday evenings. For twenty years. In a cold room. With five other people.
[whispers] You can't practise alone.
You can't. And nearly half of Britain's rings have no listed practice night at all.
Is that why they're counting?
The Council's own strategy document says sixty per cent of ringers are now over sixty. In nineteen eighty-eight, half of them were under forty.
[sighs] And the recruitment drives?

A ringer named John Harrison went through sixty-five years of one guild's membership rolls and showed each campaign's gains halved within about two years. Their programme planned about fifty-eight thousand pounds of spending last year. It spent six thousand two hundred.
[scoffs] Against a target of ten thousand new ringers.
Which is roughly three pounds forty a head.
And the local hook — please tell me there's one.
There is, and I did not expect it. There is exactly one ring of bells in all of Southeast Asia, and it is in Singapore.
[gasps] Where?

St Andrew's Cathedral. Twelve bells. The heaviest about one thousand two hundred and ninety-seven kilograms. Six of them cast in eighteen eighty-eight, the rest in twenty nineteen when an old chime was converted.
Does anyone ring them?

A local band does. Last December they rang one thousand three hundred and twenty changes of Plain Bob Doubles in forty-six minutes, and footnoted it — celebrating the birth of our Saviour with hope and joy.
[warmly] That's lovely.
One housekeeping note. The cathedral's own bells page returns an error and has been removed from the national register. So it's a Sunday visit, not a web form.
Culture. Quickly, because I want the last story.

Godzilla Minus Zero took thirty million six hundred and twelve thousand dollars across three thousand two hundred and fifty-four American screens. With subtitles. Ninety-one per cent on Rotten Tomatoes from a hundred and ninety-two critics. David Jenkins at Little White Lies: a pale, radiation-blackened shadow of the twenty twenty-three film. He says it feels rushed.
And a correction, I think.

Ours. We called the opening settled at thirty million five eight seven. Box Office Mojo now gives a slightly higher figure, and its weekend view is still flagged as an estimate. We've withdrawn the word settled.
[warmly] Good.

The Good Life: Phillips in Geneva held the first watch auction ever to pass a hundred million U.S. dollars. One F.P. Journe made eight point six eight million Swiss francs — about eight and a half times its own published estimate.
[scoffs] What's an estimate for, then?

That's our sceptic, more or less. And thirteen watches by that one living maker were a third of the entire sale. A study of eleven thousand two hundred and seventy-nine children in Pediatrics, following them from age twelve. Does troubled social-media use cause low mood, or the reverse? Both. A little. And not every year. The effects run between three and seven hundredths of a standard deviation — and every single anxiety path crossed zero.
[thoughtful] So the honest headline is 'very large study finds very small two-way effect'.

And general guidance, not medical advice. Nothing there supports reading a child's low mood as caused by a phone. A six-month trial at Surrey found a longevity supplement improved blood-vessel function by two point nine percentage points. Four of eleven outcomes cleared significance. Every blood-lipid result was null, and cholesterol moved the wrong way. The placebo group was seven years older than the treatment group.
[wry] In a trial about ageing.
A physician who wasn't involved, Brad Stanfield, put it well: it's an exciting result, but the effect size is surprisingly large, and he'd want an independent group to replicate it first.
And the diary, one line.

Gardens by the Bay opens a Studio Ghibli exhibition on the eighteenth of December — a world premiere. And January's sumo tickets go on sale on the fifth of December, at ten in the morning Japan time. The tournament running right now is sold out on every single day.
[drawn out] All right. The long read.

Mongolia. And it starts with a steel box. The tüts. A quick-service point — the kiosk that was Ulaanbaatar's street retail. The city sold them to the traders. Brown ones in twenty fifteen, white ones in twenty nineteen.
The city sold them.
And stopped collecting land fees in twenty twenty. Then in February of last year, it ordered them cleared away. About sixteen hundred.
[pause] And the people?

The city offered one thousand six hundred and sixty-nine jobs, and stalls in forty-eight markets. Twenty-two operators took a stall. Their own association surveyed more than two hundred and fifty members and put their combined debts above thirty billion tögrög. It was never a shop. It was a leveraged livelihood.
And what replaced them?
A Korean convenience franchise. Twenty-one stores in twenty eighteen. Six hundred and three by the middle of this year.
So it's a Korean-wave story.
That's the joke people make — they call the capital Mongtan, Mongolia crossed with a Korean new town. And I think the joke is wrong.
[curious] Why?
Read what the chain actually supplies. Its own prospectus offers customers free access to toilets, shelter in an emergency, a resting point in summer's heat and winter's chill.
That's not retail. That's infrastructure.

It calls itself social infrastructure for the daily life of the community. Add a cold chain, a food factory doing sixty thousand meals a day, parcel lockers, tax receipts. When municipal rubbish collection fell behind in one district, the company signed its own agreement with the district governor and shifted six hundred and eight tonnes of waste.
[whispers] So the company is doing the council's job.
Now look at the four faults the city named against the kiosks. Stealing electricity. Selling uncertified goods. Polluting. Blocking pavements.
[pause] And a franchise is certified against all four.

Metered power. Hazard certification. A licensed waste contract. A shopfront inside the building line. The city's compliance agenda and the chain's commercial interest are the same agenda, written once.
So it isn't taste. It's —

Legibility. The state chose the retail form it can tax, inspect, insure and count. The company ranks sixty-fifth in the country by tax paid and second — second in the whole country — by number of insured employees.
[thoughtful] That's what formalisation looks like from a treasury.
And a development bank has now lent it ten million dollars, calling a convenience-store chain food-security infrastructure.
Does the essay let the chain off?
No. Four things cut against us, and we printed all of them. Nobody has measured a single kiosk closure caused by competition. We could not find one figure, or one independent study.
So what can you say?
A sequence. The city sold them the boxes, waived the fees, and cleared them. That's reportable. Causation isn't.
And where does it end?
With a number in the company's own half-year report. At the stores open through both periods, the average basket — what a customer actually spends — fell one point six per cent.
[drawn out] It's shrinking.
Two years ago it was growing seven per cent in real terms. The formalisation is almost complete, and the thing being formalised has stopped growing.
[drawn out] A country can swap a kiosk economy for a convenience-store economy.
But it cannot franchise demand.
[pause] And the operators?
They say the city is bringing in a third generation of kiosk now. Glass ones. They offered to clean them and to pay tax, and were refused.
[whispers] Whatever that is, it isn't a market.
That's the last line of the essay, more or less.
[exhales] One thread through the whole book, then. Who's keeping score, and who are they scoring.
The suppliers are buying the offering. The city cleared the traders it had sold the boxes to. And a few thousand English ringers are going to count themselves on Monday because nobody made them.
[warmly] That's the one I'll remember.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
